claims.statement: Fifty million dollars. That was the price... Everyone who has told this story agrees on that number.
claims.evidence: Randolph (Fortune 2023 / Vanity Fair 2019 excerpt), Hastings (Marketplace 2020 via Stratrix) and Antioco (LinkedIn Dec 2021: 'apparently offered to sell their company for $50 million') all name $50M. Script avoids calling it a firm sale offer.

claims.statement: Today, that start-up is Netflix, worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
claims.evidence: Market cap about $293B on 13-14 Oct 2026 (StockAnalysis: share price $70.57 at close 14 Oct 2026; market-cap summaries $292.7-293.8B). 'Hundreds of billions' is the conservative wording.

claims.statement: It is down to one last store, in Oregon. / one franchised Blockbuster... In Bend, Oregon.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia Blockbuster: only one franchised store remains, in Bend, Oregon (since 2018/2019). Randolph himself: 'the company that once had 9,000 stores, is down to a single one' (Fortune).

claims.statement: This is where Blockbuster was born, back in nineteen eighty-five.
claims.evidence: First Blockbuster store opened 19 Oct 1985 in Dallas, founder David Cook.

claims.statement: Close to five billion dollars a year in revenue. / revenue still growing, up about eleven percent / $50M was about one percent of yearly revenue.
claims.evidence: Blockbuster FY2001 10-K (opened): 2001 revenue 'over $5.1 billion', 'increased about 4.0% from 2000' -> 2000 about $4.96B. Viacom FY2000 10-K (SEC full-text excerpt via search, page not fully read): Blockbuster revenue $4,960.1M in 2000 vs $4,463.5M in 1999 = +11.1%. 10-K also cites 'four consecutive years of same store revenue growth'. $50M / $4.96B = 1.0%.

claims.statement: Thousands of stores.
claims.evidence: FY2001 10-K: 7,981 stores at 31 Dec 2001 (4,393+981 US, 2,019+588 intl) after a net addition of 304 in 2001 -> 7,677 at end 2000; company-operated 6,412 after +158 -> 6,254 at end 2000.

claims.statement: Its parent company is the media giant Viacom. / Blockbuster answered to Viacom.
claims.evidence: Viacom parent 1994-2004 (Wikipedia infobox); 1999 IPO sold only 18% (Wikipedia Antioco); FY2001 10-K shows 144,000,000 Class B shares (Viacom). 'Whether Antioco could have bought Netflix on his own, we simply don't know' is correctly framed as unknown.

claims.statement: He spent around twenty years at the convenience chain Seven-Eleven, then worked at Circle K, before he took the top job at Blockbuster.
claims.evidence: 20 years at 7-Eleven (1970-1990) is correct. But the sequence is incomplete in a misleading way: 7-Eleven -> Pearle Vision COO (1990) -> Circle K president/CEO (1991-1996) -> Taco Bell CEO (1996-1997) -> Blockbuster CEO (July 1997). He came to Blockbuster from Taco Bell, not from Circle K.
claims.fix: He spent around twenty years at the convenience chain Seven-Eleven, then ran Circle K and later Taco Bell, before he took the top job at Blockbuster in nineteen ninety-seven.

claims.statement: Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph founded Netflix in nineteen ninety-seven, in a small town called Scotts Valley.
claims.evidence: Prospectus: incorporated in Delaware in August 1997; Fortune: Randolph co-founded Netflix with Hastings in 1997. Scotts Valley per research s1 (Wikipedia Netflix, page did not render fully in this check; long-established fact).

claims.statement: Meeting at Blockbuster's headquarters; three visitors: Hastings, Randolph and finance chief Barry McCarthy.
claims.evidence: Variety 2025 (via Stratrix): 'everyone agrees there was a meeting at Blockbuster's Dallas headquarters'. Randolph's memoir places himself, Hastings and CFO Barry McCarthy at the table. Script does not put Antioco in the room.

claims.statement: Since September nineteen ninety-nine, customers pay a flat monthly subscription.
claims.evidence: Prospectus: 'Our subscription service has grown rapidly since its launch in September 1999.'

claims.statement: By the end of the following year, about twenty-five million American households will own a DVD player, nearly double the year before. That year, Americans will spend twenty-one billion dollars renting and buying videos.
claims.evidence: Prospectus (Adams Media Research): ~25M US households had a set-top DVD player at end of 2001, +91% in 2001; consumer video rentals and purchases $21B in 2001 (domestic). Blockbuster 10-K (Kagan): DVD households 'nearly doubled during 2001'.

claims.statement: About three hundred thousand subscribers. Revenue thirty-five point nine million dollars. Net loss fifty-seven point four million.
claims.evidence: Prospectus summary data, FY2000: total revenues $35,894K; operating loss $57,557K; net loss $57,363K; subscribers 292K (unaudited).

claims.statement: You would be paying fifty million dollars for a business that had just burned through more than fifty million dollars.
claims.evidence: $57.4M is the FULL-YEAR 2000 loss. The meeting took place during 2000 (Hastings: early 2000; Randolph/Wikipedia: Sept 2000), so at the moment of decision the company had not yet 'burned through' that amount. Hindsight slip in the fairness section. The preceding sentence ('lost more money in that one year than the price') and the freeze line are fine.
claims.fix: You would be paying fifty million dollars for a business on its way to losing more than fifty million dollars that year.

claims.statement: Second, the mood. The dot-com bubble was bursting.
claims.evidence: No claim id in the research. Wikipedia: the bubble peaked on 10 March 2000 and then fell. If the meeting was 'early 2000' (Hastings), the bubble had not yet burst; the meeting date is disputed (c14).
claims.fix: Second, the mood. In two thousand, the dot-com bubble peaked and began to burst. (Add claim c54: Nasdaq/dot-com peak 10 Mar 2000, source Wikipedia Dot-com bubble.)

claims.statement: Fifty million dollars was about one percent of Blockbuster's yearly revenue. / about nine hundred times the fifty million.
In his twenty nineteen book, That Will Never Work, he recalls Antioco struggling not to laugh.
claims.evidence: Vanity Fair book excerpt, Sept 2019, headline: He 'Was Struggling Not to Laugh': Inside Netflix's Crazy, Doomed Meeting With Blockbuster. Correctly attributed as Randolph's recollection.

claims.statement: In twenty twenty-three, he reportedly said Blockbuster 'laughed us out of the room.'
claims.evidence: Fortune, 14 Apr 2023 (Steve Mollman): Blockbuster executives 'laughed us out of the room,' Randolph recalled on Twitter. Flagged as Randolph's memory. Optional: 'reportedly' can become 'he wrote on Twitter'.

claims.statement: In twenty twenty-one, he wrote on LinkedIn: 'I can say with complete confidence that there were never any serious acquisition talks in 2000.' He says he wasn't even part of the meeting. He only stopped by to greet the guests.
claims.evidence: Antioco LinkedIn post 23 Dec 2021, quoted verbatim in Stratrix source list: 'I can say with complete confidence that there were never any serious acquisition talks in 2000. ... I was not a part of that meeting, although I did stop by to greet our guests.' Opening line also visible on LinkedIn (research s9).

claims.statement: And Reed Hastings? He has reportedly said he doesn't think it was serious. More curiosity than anything else.
claims.evidence: Variety, 21 Mar 2025, as quoted by Stratrix: 'They had us down there, but I don't think it was serious. I think it was curiosity rather than anything else.' Secondhand (Variety page not readable), correctly hedged with 'reportedly' and paraphrased, not quoted.

claims.statement: Almost everything else about this meeting is disputed. Even the month. / Dallas, two thousand.
claims.evidence: Hastings (Marketplace 2020 via Stratrix): early 2000; Wikipedia Antioco / Randolph: September 2000. Script keeps to 'two thousand'.

claims.statement: On the twenty-ninth of May, two thousand and two, it went public.
claims.evidence: Prospectus dated 22 May 2002; NFLX began trading on Nasdaq on 23 May 2002 (Benzinga 'This Day in Market History, May 23: Netflix Goes Public'). 29 May 2002 is only the closing/delivery date of the shares (prospectus: 'ready for delivery on or about May 29, 2002'; FY2002 10-K: 'on May 29, 2002, the Company closed the sale').
claims.fix: In May two thousand and two, it went public. (or: On the twenty-third of May, two thousand and two, its shares started trading.)

claims.statement: Fifteen dollars a share. Eighty-two and a half million dollars raised. Valued at roughly three hundred and ten million dollars. About six times the number it had named in Dallas.
claims.evidence: Prospectus: 5,500,000 shares at $15.00 = $82,500,000; 20,648,074 shares outstanding after the offering x $15 = $309.7M (excludes options/warrants and the later 825,000-share over-allotment). $310M / $50M = 6.2.

claims.statement: More than six hundred thousand subscribers, about double what it had in two thousand, more than eleven and a half thousand titles, nineteen dollars and ninety-five cents a month.
claims.evidence: Prospectus: 'more than 600,000 subscribers', 'more than 11,500 ... titles', standard plan '$19.95 per month'; subscribers 603K at 31 Mar 2002 vs 292K at end 2000 = 2.07x.

claims.statement: In two thousand and four, it hit its peak: nine thousand and ninety-four stores.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (citing SEC): at its peak in 2004 Blockbuster employed 84,300 people and operated 9,094 stores.

claims.statement: That same year it split from Viacom and launched its own online rental service, Blockbuster Online.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: spun off from Viacom on or around 14 Oct 2004; Blockbuster Online introduced 2004. NBC (May 2005): 'Last year, Blockbuster spent more than $200 million to launch its own mail-order online service.'

claims.statement: In January two thousand and five, it dropped most late fees.
claims.evidence: Blockbuster 2005 10-Q (via SEC search excerpt): 'end of late fees' program implemented 1 Jan 2005 at US company-operated stores (franchisees optional, hence 'most'). Wikipedia: 'Antioco scrapped late fees in January'.

claims.statement: In two thousand and five, Blockbuster reported a net loss of five hundred and eighty-eight million dollars. More than half of that was a write-down.
claims.evidence: Blockbuster FY2006 results release: 2005 net loss $588.1M; 2005 included a $341.9M non-cash charge to impair goodwill and other long-lived assets (58%).

claims.statement: That same year [2005], the activist investor Carl Icahn bought a stake of nearly ten percent.
claims.evidence: Icahn's Schedule 13D/A (Amendment 2): purchases began 11 Nov 2004; original 13D filed 14 Dec 2004; by 7 Apr 2005 he held 9.70% of Class A and 7.73% of Class B. NBC, 10 May 2005: 'owns nearly 10 percent'; he won board seats in the May 2005 proxy fight. The stake was built mostly in late 2004, not 'that same year' (2005).
claims.fix: By then, the activist investor Carl Icahn had built a stake of nearly ten percent, and in May two thousand and five he won a seat on the board.

claims.statement: Then, in the autumn of two thousand and six, came Total Access. Rent your discs online, then return them to a Blockbuster store and swap them for free.
claims.evidence: Blockbuster release 27 Feb 2007: 'five months since we launched our new integrated offering'; Total Access lets online customers return DVDs by mail or exchange them at a participating store for free in-store rentals.

claims.statement: About two point two million subscribers, seven hundred thousand added in the last three months; back in profit: fifty-four point seven million dollars.
claims.evidence: Release 27 Feb 2007: ~2.2M online subscribers (~2M paying) at end 2006; ~700,000 added in Q4 2006; 2006 net income $54.7M (operating income $79.1M). Note: net income includes a $76.4M tax benefit (pre-tax loss $8.5M); 'back in profit' is accurate on both net and operating level.

claims.statement: Antioco says Total Access brought Netflix back to the table... That is his account. Nobody else has confirmed it.
claims.evidence: First part is correctly attributed (Antioco, LinkedIn Pulse June 2022, via Stratrix). 'Nobody else has confirmed it' is an unverifiable negative claim; Wikipedia's Blockbuster article independently reports that in 2007 Hastings approached Antioco with a suggestion to buy Blockbuster's online business.
claims.fix: Delete 'Nobody else has confirmed it.' Keep: 'That is his account.'

claims.statement: Board offered a bonus of 2.28 million; he said he was owed 7.65 million. In March, they settled. Exit payment just under five million instead of thirteen and a half million.
claims.evidence: Release 27 Feb 2007: board exercised negative discretion on 25 Jan 2007, $2.28M; CEO claims $7.65M. 8-K 19 Mar 2007: settlement; lump sum $4.9875M vs $13.5M under previous agreement; 2006 bonus $3.0525M. Optional precision: 'lump-sum exit payment' (Wikipedia reports a larger total severance package).

claims.statement: Antioco left, and Jim Keyes took over as CEO that same year.
claims.evidence: Blockbuster press release 2 Jul 2007: James W. Keyes appointed Chairman and CEO effective that day, replacing John F. Antioco.

claims.statement: Also in two thousand and seven, Netflix started streaming.
claims.evidence: Netflix 'Watch Now' announced 15 Jan 2007, launched 16 Jan 2007 (Quartz, Wikipedia Timeline of Netflix).

claims.statement: On the twenty-third of September, two thousand and ten, Blockbuster filed for Chapter Eleven.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'On September 23, 2010, Blockbuster filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection'.

claims.statement: In two thousand and eleven, Dish Network bought Blockbuster out of bankruptcy, with about one thousand seven hundred stores. The last company-owned stores closed in early two thousand and fourteen.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: Dish won the auction 6 Apr 2011, completed 26 Apr 2011, 'its remaining 1,700 stores'; Dish closed all 300 remaining corporate stores between 6 Nov 2013 and 12 Jan 2014.

claims.statement: In two thousand and twenty-five, it brought in forty-five point two billion dollars in revenue.
claims.evidence: Netflix Q4 2025 shareholder letter (Jan 2026), reported by TheDesk/Deadline/S&P: 2025 revenue $45.2B (+16%), operating income $13.3B, net income $11.0B.

claims.statement: LESSON section (two practical lessons).
claims.evidence: No factual claims. Structure: channel brief requires ONE short practical lesson; the section contains two (value the threat if it wins + fund the transition).
claims.fix: Keep one lesson, e.g. only: 'When a small company could one day replace your core business, don't only ask what it's worth today; ask what it would cost you if it wins.'

issues: AFTERMATH, IPO date is wrong: 'On the twenty-ninth of May, two thousand and two, it went public.' NFLX began trading on 23 May 2002; 29 May was only the closing date. Fix: 'In May two thousand and two, it went public.' (or 'On the twenty-third of May, two thousand and two, its shares started trading.')

AFTERMATH, Icahn timing is wrong: 'That same year, the activist investor Carl Icahn bought a stake of nearly ten percent.' His 13D shows he started buying on 11 Nov 2004, filed on 14 Dec 2004, and held 9.7% of Class A by Apr 2005. Fix: 'By then, the activist investor Carl Icahn had built a stake of nearly ten percent, and in May two thousand and five he won a seat on the board.'

AFTERMATH, unsupported negative claim: 'That is his account. Nobody else has confirmed it.' This cannot be verified, and Wikipedia reports a 2007 Hastings approach to Antioco. Fix: delete 'Nobody else has confirmed it.' and keep 'That is his account.'

PRESSURE, hindsight slip: 'You would be paying fifty million dollars for a business that had just burned through more than fifty million dollars.' The $57.4M is the full-year 2000 loss, and the meeting happened during 2000. Fix: 'You would be paying fifty million dollars for a business on its way to losing more than fifty million dollars that year.'

PRESSURE, no claim id and date-sensitive: 'The dot-com bubble was bursting.' The bubble peaked on 10 Mar 2000, and the meeting date is disputed (Hastings says early 2000). Fix: 'In two thousand, the dot-com bubble peaked and began to burst.' Add claim c54 (source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dot-com_bubble).

SET THE SCENE, misleading career sequence: 'then worked at Circle K, before he took the top job at Blockbuster.' Antioco came to Blockbuster from Taco Bell (CEO 1996-97), after Pearle Vision and Circle K. Fix: 'then ran Circle K and later Taco Bell, before he took the top job at Blockbuster in nineteen ninety-seven.'

LESSON, structure: the brief asks for ONE short lesson, but the section has two ('ask what it would cost you if it wins' plus 'fund it and see it through'). Fix: keep only the first sentence (or merge both into one sentence).
notes: The story holds up: no reject grounds. The $50M figure, the disputed nature of the meeting and all quotes are correctly hedged. The fairness section is strong. Re-opened and verified: Netflix 424B4 prospectus (2000 revenue, loss, subscribers, IPO terms, 2002 subscribers/titles/price, DVD market data), Blockbuster FY2001 10-K (2000 stores 7,677 / 6,254 company-operated, and 2000 revenue about $4.96B derived from the +4.0% 2001 growth; c22 and c23 can be upgraded to verified), Blockbuster FY2006 results release, the Antioco settlement 8-K of 19 Mar 2007, the Keyes appointment release of 2 Jul 2007, the Icahn 13D/A, the Fortune 2023 'laughed us out of the room' piece, the Vanity Fair 2019 excerpt headline, the Stratrix page with the verbatim Antioco LinkedIn quote, Wikipedia (Blockbuster, Antioco, Dot-com bubble), NBC 2005 (Icahn nearly 10%), and Netflix 2025 results and current market cap (about $293B on 13-14 Oct 2026). Caveats: the +11% revenue growth for 2000 rests on a SEC full-text excerpt of Viacom's FY2000 10-K ($4,960.1M vs $4,463.5M), not a fully read page. Hastings's 'curiosity' remark is secondhand (Variety via Stratrix) and is properly hedged. Optional polish (not blocking): (a) 'he reportedly said' can become 'he wrote on Twitter' (Fortune confirms the tweet); (b) 'His exit payment' could be 'His lump-sum exit payment', because reports of the total severance package are higher; (c) 2006 net income of $54.7M included a $76.4M tax benefit, but operating income ($79.1M) was positive too, so 'back in profit' stands. Structure: freeze at about 43%, reveal, numbers, verdict line and word count (~1,540 words, ~9:20) are all in range. After the 7 fixes above this script can pass without another full check.
